questions.prompt: Which opponent is closest to YOU?

options.text: Gold 1
The far blue line
The centre-ice faceoff dot

questions.explanation: Gold 1 is the shown nearby opponent. Check the actual route rather than assuming the boards or reverse are sealed.

questions.prompt: Which two facts belong in the reverse decision?

options.text: Whether D2 can receive across the middle
Gold 1’s pressure near YOU
Whether W has already received the reverse

questions.explanation: Pressure and the possible receiver both matter. W has not been assigned possession.

questions.prompt: Put one cautious reverse routine in order.

options.text: Check the far-side support
Protect the puck from Gold 1
Reverse only if the new lane is usable

questions.explanation: Protection buys a second look; checking D2 tells you whether the reverse helps; if D2 is covered, keep possession and choose another exit.

questions.prompt: Move D2 to compare another support angle across the middle.
questions.explanation: The example moves D2 closer to YOU. Check the net, pressure and passing route before considering a reverse.

questions.prompt: If D2 is covered before the reverse, what should YOU reconsider?

options.text: Whether a protected hold or another support player is safer
Reversing anyway because the first lane was closed
Leaving the puck for the first teammate who calls

questions.explanation: D2’s coverage removes the intended receiver, so protection or a different support read preserves possession; if D2 reopens, the reverse can become available.

questions.prompt: What would you tell D2 before using the reverse?
questions.explanation: Call the pressure side and far-side support picture so D2 knows whether to present or stay low; if the call changes, the reverse decision changes too.

questions.prompt: Which player has the puck?

options.text: D1
YOU
Gold 1

questions.explanation: The puck is assigned to D1, so your job is support; if possession changes, the support read resets.

questions.prompt: Which two details make YOU a useful hinge?

options.text: A visible lane between D1 and D2
Separation that leaves a reachable support angle
Standing directly on D1’s route

questions.explanation: A separated middle lane connects the defenders and leaves D1 room to carry; standing on D1’s route removes the support option.

questions.prompt: Order one hinge-support read.

options.text: See D1’s pressure
Show a middle passing lane
Adjust if Gold 1 closes it

questions.explanation: Pressure determines room; showing the lane gives a second outlet; a closed lane requires a new angle.

questions.prompt: Move YOU into an example hinge lane inside Gold 1 and clear of D1’s puck route.
questions.explanation: The inside spot gives D1 a support angle without copying the corner route; it is farther from D1 than the starting spot, so it is not a guaranteed short connection.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 steps into the middle lane, what is a useful change?

options.text: Slide to a new support angle while D1 protects the puck
Stay hidden behind Gold 1 and call for a pass
Skate through D1’s stick lane

questions.explanation: Gold 1’s move changes the route. Compare another angle while checking possession and other support.

questions.prompt: How does your support help D1 even when D1 does not pass?
questions.explanation: An available support option may change the defender’s choices. It does not force Gold 1 to react or guarantee extra time for D1.

questions.prompt: How are YOU and D2 positioned along the length of the rink?

options.text: At the same depth near centre ice
D1 is behind the net
Gold 2 is below the goal line

questions.explanation: YOU and D2 share the same depth but are separated across the rink. This alone does not prove one defender covers both.

questions.prompt: Which two changes could create a connected second option?

options.text: Move YOU closer to Navy’s net than D2
Keep a lane between YOU and D1
Both forwards skate to the same dot

questions.explanation: A height change separates reads and a connecting lane keeps the regroup playable; one dot removes separation.

questions.prompt: Arrange one staggered support response.

options.text: Read Gold 1’s middle shade
Compare a different depth from D2
Present the lane D1 can see

questions.explanation: Gold 1’s shade sets the need for space; changing height makes a second picture; presenting where D1 can see turns spacing into support.

questions.prompt: Move YOU wider and closer to Navy’s net than D2.
questions.explanation: The example changes width and depth. It is farther from D1 than the starting spot, so check whether the connection remains useful.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 follows your drop, what should YOU notice?

options.text: D2 may now be the open higher outlet
YOU are now the best return option
D2 is still covered exactly as before

questions.explanation: Gold 1’s movement can uncover D2’s height, so update the lane; if D2 is covered too, reset the regroup.

questions.prompt: How could changing depth alter D1’s options?
questions.explanation: It changes the passing angle and spacing. Width can also be useful; compare the actual pressure and accessible lanes.

questions.prompt: Which lane is F1 trying to occupy?

options.text: The middle lane
The left corner behind the net
The wide lane beside YOU

questions.explanation: F1’s stated middle drive identifies the lane; support should protect a separate option beside it.

questions.prompt: Which two jobs fit your wide support?

options.text: Stay outside Gold 1’s inside position
Keep a passing angle back to F1
Cut directly through F1’s path

questions.explanation: Width gives F1 room and a visible release; crossing the route removes both options.

questions.prompt: Put one entry-support read in order.

options.text: Identify Gold 1’s inside position
Hold width beside F1’s drive
Adjust when lane or puck changes

questions.explanation: The defender’s inside position sets width; holding it gives F1 room; a changed lane requires a new route.

questions.prompt: Move YOU wider while staying closer to the blue line than F1.
questions.explanation: The example maintains separation from F1’s middle route. Check the defenders and lane before calling for the puck.

questions.prompt: If Gold 2 steps into your wall-side lane, what is the next useful read?

options.text: Whether D2 can become safer high support
Whether to skate through F1
Whether the defender no longer matters

questions.explanation: Gold 2 removes the first support lane, so D2’s height matters; if D2 is covered, hold space and avoid crowding F1.

questions.prompt: How can wide support help a middle drive without receiving the puck?
questions.explanation: Width stretches Gold 1 and leaves F1 a release or carry lane; if the defence stays narrow, the wide lane may become the next pass.

questions.prompt: Where are YOU relative to W?

options.text: Closer to the attacking goal line than W
Above W at the point
Behind Gold 1 at centre ice

questions.explanation: Your location creates the low cycle option; moving level with W changes that relationship.

questions.prompt: Which two relationships help a low cycle?

options.text: A possible outlet toward the goal line
D2 staying high enough to balance
W and YOU must both drop below the goal line

questions.explanation: The low lane moves the puck away from pressure while D2 balances above; crowding removes the next option.

questions.prompt: Order one low-cycle support check.

options.text: See whether W can protect the puck
Compare support toward the goal line
Reassess D2’s high balance

questions.explanation: W’s control decides whether a cycle exists; low support gives a release; checking D2 prevents an exposed point.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a point nearer the goal line and middle than W.
questions.explanation: Relative to W, the example is nearer the goal line and slightly nearer the middle. Both Gold defenders still affect whether a short pass is usable.

questions.prompt: If Gold 2 drops below W, what should YOU reconsider?

options.text: Whether the low lane is still open or higher support is safer
Cycling into Gold 2 because the puck is nearby
Leaving D2 with no balance

questions.explanation: Gold 2’s drop changes the low lane, so read coverage before moving; if it stays open, keep it available without forcing.

questions.prompt: What must W see before using your low option?
questions.explanation: W needs your separation from Gold 2 and a reachable lane without a blind pass; if pressure closes it, protect and wait for D2.
